title: Synchronized Quantum Devices in Lossy Channels
authors: Ravi Singh Adhikari, Aman Gupta, Xiaoyu Ai, Robert Malaney
abstract: Due to their tight temporal coupling, entangled photon pairs produced by spontaneous parametric down-conversion offer a new route to improved network synchronization among quantum-enabled devices. In the emerging space-based quantum internet, such synchronization will be pivotal to operational success. Here, we propose and experimentally demonstrate a new polarization-assisted protocol that allows quantum-enabled devices to remain synchronized under the high loss conditions anticipated for satellite-to-ground quantum channels. Our experimental results show that polarization assistance extends reliable synchronization acquisition to higher channel losses and an increase of up to 40$\%$ in satellite-to-ground distance. Supporting Monte Carlo simulations show that this performance improvement extends over a wide range of photon-starved conditions. Collectively, these results not only provide a proof of concept for polarization-assisted network synchronization but also demonstrate its pragmatic importance in significantly extending the range under which quantum-enabled devices forming the backbone of the quantum internet can remain highly synchronized.
summary: This paper introduces a polarization-assisted protocol to enhance clock synchronization for quantum devices communicating over lossy channels like satellite links. By exploiting polarization correlations, the method effectively suppresses background noise that plagues standard timing measurements. This results in a significant extension of the operational range, proving its practical importance for the quantum internet.
main_problem: The core challenge is achieving reliable clock synchronization for quantum devices operating over high-loss, long-distance quantum channels, such as satellite-to-ground links.
main_result: The proposed polarization-assisted protocol significantly improves synchronization robustness, extending the reliable operational range by up to 40% compared to methods relying only on temporal coincidence measurements.
method: The authors compare a temporal-only estimation method against a polarization-assisted estimator, which uses polarization post-selection to suppress background noise.
model_or_system: The system involves entangled photon pairs generated via SPDC and distributed over free-space channels. The analysis models the timing error ($\Delta t$) and compares the performance of estimators based on time-only versus polarization-resolved coincidence counts.
key_observables: Synchronization-acquisition probability ($P_{	ext{succ},l}$), Fisher Information ($I$), and the clock offset ($	au$).
important_parameters: Channel loss ($\eta$), background count rate ($R_b$), and the visibility ($V$) of the entangled source.
main_assumptions: Timing errors are assumed to be independent Gaussian variables, and the temporal statistics are assumed independent of the polarization statistics.
figures_summary: Figure 5 compares temporal-only vs. polarization-assisted histograms, showing the polarization method reveals a clear peak obscured by noise in the former. Figure 6 quantifies the increased loss threshold ($\eta_{90}$) achieved by the polarization-assisted estimator.
paper_structure: The paper develops the theoretical framework by deriving performance metrics (like Fisher Information) for both estimators, analyzes the improvement in the strongly background-dominated limit, and culminates in experimental/simulation results demonstrating the extended operational range in high-loss regimes.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the practical limitations of quantum networking by providing a concrete, experimentally validated technique to maintain synchronization in noisy, lossy channels, which is crucial for scaling quantum internet infrastructure.

Fig. 2: Experimental setup for the polarization-assisted clock-synchronization proof-of-concept. The entangled-photon source (EPS) generates polarization- entangled photon pairs, which are routed through the free-space optical chan- nel using mirrors M1–M2. A variable attenuator (VA) introduces controlled channel loss symmetrically at Alice’s and Bob’s stations to emulate high- loss satellite-channel conditions. At Alice and Bob, polarizing beam splitters (PBSs) separate the horizontal (H) and vertical (V) polarization components, which are detected by single-photon counting modules D1–D4. See main text for the setup of TT1 and TT2.

Fig. 3: Experimental synchronization-acquisition probability, Psucc,l, as a function of total channel loss, η. Blue and orange denote background- count rates of Rb = 1.5kHz and Rb = 70kHz, respectively. Curves are logistic least-squares fits. Stars denote the fitted synchronization-acquisition loss thresholds for Psucc,l = 0.9.

Fig. 3 presents the experimentally extracted synchronization-acquisition probability for the temporal-only and polarization-assisted estimators at two background-count rates, Rb = 1.5kHz and Rb = 70kHz, representative of low-background and high-background operating conditions, respectively, as a function of η ranging from 45–68dB. At lower total channel loss, both estimators reliably recover the clock offset. As the total channel loss increases, the temporal-only estimator transitions from reliable to unreliable acquisition, whereas polarization post-selection shifts this transition toward higher total channel loss.
